extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent agents, and legal practitioners dealing with UK patent law and Patent Office practice (late 19th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory and procedural rules governing patent applications, Patent Office administration, international priority claims, evidentiary effects, and the registration/examination of patent agents under the UK Patents Acts (primarily 1883 and 1888) and the International Convention (Paris, 1883).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describing oneself as a Patent Agent when not registered
rubrics_metrics.description: By the first section of the Act of 1888 it is enacted that any person describing himself to be a Patent Agent when he is not on the register is liable on summary conviction to a penalty of 20l. (See Chapter XXIV., 'On the Institute of Patent Agents.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After July 1st, 1889 a person shall not describe himself as a Patent Agent by advertisement, by description on his place of business, by any document issued by him, or otherwise, unless he is registered as a Patent Agent in pursuance of that Act; any person knowingly contravening this provision is liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding 20l. The Board of Trade may make rules giving effect to this enactment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction for summary conviction offences
rubrics_metrics.description: In Scotland any offence under the Act of 1883 declared to be punishable on summary conviction may be prosecuted in the Sheriff's Court. In the Isle of Man any offence under the Act which would in England be punishable on summary conviction may be prosecuted, and any fine in respect thereof recovered at the instance of the person aggrieved, in the manner in which offences punishable on summary conviction may for the time being be prosecuted. (Sect. 108; Sect. 112, subsect. 3.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies territorial/procedural venues for summary conviction offences under the Act in Scotland and the Isle of Man.

rubrics_metrics.name: False entries in registers and false documentary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The ninety-third section of the Act of 1883 enacts that if any person makes or causes to be made a false entry in any Register kept under the Act, or a writing falsely purporting to be a copy of an entry in any such register, or produces or tenders, or causes to be produced or tendered, in evidence, any such writing, knowing the entry or writing to be false, he shall be guilty of a misdemeanor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Isle of Man the punishment for a misdemeanor under the Act is imprisonment for any term not exceeding two years, with or without hard labour, and with or without a fine not exceeding 100l. at the discretion of the Court. This provision criminalises falsification of official patent registers and the use of forged copies in evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: International Convention — right of priority (six months)
rubrics_metrics.description: By Article I any person who has duly registered and made an application for a patent in one of the contracting states shall enjoy, as regards registration in the other states, a right of priority for six months, an additional month being allowed for countries beyond sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A subsequent registration (i.e., a patent obtained on a subsequent application) in any of the other states of the Union before expiry of that period shall not be invalidated by acts done in the interval, either by registration, by publication of the invention, or the working of it by a third party. The clause is subject to conditions and time-limits set by the Convention and implementing national rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convention applications in the UK — time, form and required documents
rubrics_metrics.description: According to present regulations, 'Patents (International and Colonial Arrangements) Rules 24-29, 1890,' an application in the United Kingdom for a patent under the International Convention must be made within seven months from the date of the first foreign application, and must be signed by the person or persons by whom such first foreign application was made. It must be made upon form A2 (stamped II...), and, in addition to the specification, provisional or complete, must be accompanied by (1) a copy or copies of the specification and drawings as filed in the Patent Office of the Foreign State or British Possession in respect of the first foreign application, duly certified by the official chief of such Patent Office, or otherwise verified to the satisfaction of the Comptroller; (2) a statutory declaration as to the identity of the invention ... and, if the specification be in a foreign language, a translation thereof must be annexed to and verified by statutory declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent under the International Convention can only be granted to the person who has made the foreign application. The UK implementing rules require certified copies, statutory declarations of identity, and translations verified by statutory declaration; the specified seven-month period aligns with the Convention priority period as implemented in UK practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement to damages limited until acceptance of complete specification
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee under this section will not be allowed to recover damages for infringements happening prior to the date of the actual acceptance of his complete specification in this country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where priority is claimed from a foreign application, recovery of damages in the UK is measured from the date of actual acceptance of the complete specification in the UK, not from the foreign filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Convention provisions by Order in Council
rubrics_metrics.description: These provisions are only to apply to those foreign states with respect to which Her Majesty shall from time to time by Order in Council declare them to be applicable, and so long only in the case of each state as the Order in Council shall continue in force with respect to that state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Executive (Order in Council) determines which foreign states are treated as members for the UK's implementation of the Convention; effect of Convention is thus contingent on domestic Orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary protection for inventions at international exhibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporary protection is to be granted under Article 11 to patentable inventions appearing at official or officially recognised international exhibitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a limited protective regime for exhibits, preventing loss of novelty through display at recognised exhibitions (subject to Convention terms and national implementing rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Importation of articles from Union states and working obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 5 declares that the introduction by the patentee into the country where the patent has been granted of articles manufactured in any of the states of the Union shall not entail forfeiture of the patent... but the patentee shall remain bound to work his patent in those states where the law of the country obliges him to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although importation of foreign-made goods will not automatically forfeit the patent, patentees must still comply with any local 'working' obligations imposed by national law in countries where the patent is in force.

rubrics_metrics.name: International Office and publications (Bureau International)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 13 directed that an International Office should be organised under the name of Bureau International ... and that this office should be placed under the authority of the Central Administration of the Swiss Confederation, and worked under its supervision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The International Office (Le Bureau International) publishes periodicals (e.g., La Propriété Industrielle) and acts as an administrative organ of the Convention; subscription/publication details are provided (e.g., yearly subscription amount and ordering).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comptroller-General — general powers and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comptroller-General of Patents, Designs, and Trade-Marks is an officer appointed by the Board of Trade ... to act under the superintendence and direction of the Board as chief of the Patent Office ... Besides acting as general manager ... he has many important duties ... in regard to the various steps to be taken on applications for patents, on oppositions to grants, on the issue of patents, on applications for extensions of time, and on applications for leave to amend specifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duties include issuing Illustrated Journal and Reports, keeping copies of all complete specifications for sale, maintaining indexes and abridgments, and preparing other works. He is empowered to refuse patents when use would be contrary to law or morality (Sect.86), correct clerical errors, amend documents and correct irregularities (Rule 16), enlarge prescribed times (Rule 51), and dispense with acts/documents/evidence with Board sanction (Rule 80). Under s.8 (Act of 1885) he may extend times for leaving or accepting complete specifications and for sealing patents. Section 94 requires that discretionary powers not be exercised adversely to an applicant without opportunity to be heard; Section 95 allows application to law officers in cases of doubt; Section 102 requires an annual report to Parliament; Section 82(4) permits authorised officers to act during the Comptroller's absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board of Trade power to make general rules (Patents Rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board of Trade was empowered by the 101st section of the Act of 1883 to make rules for regulating generally the business of the Patent Office and all things placed under the direction and control of the Comptroller or of the Board; and particularly for regulating the practice of registration; for making or requiring duplicates of specifications, amendments, drawings, and other documents; for securing and regulating the publishing and selling of copies thereof; for securing and regulating the making, printing, publishing, and selling of indexes to abridgments of specifications and other documents in the Patent Office, and providing for the inspection of indexes, abridgments, and other documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such general rules are to be of the same effect as if they were contained in the Act, and are to be judicially noticed. They must be laid before both Houses of Parliament and can be annulled within a limited time. Consolidated rules have been issued as the Patents Rules 1890.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seal of the Patent Office and evidentiary effect of certified copies
rubrics_metrics.description: By the eighty-fourth section ... directed that there shall be a seal for the Patent Office, and that impressions thereof shall be judicially noticed. By the eighty-ninth section ... printed or written copies or extracts, purporting to be certified by the Comptroller and sealed with the seal of the Patent Office ... shall be admitted in evidence in all Courts and in all proceedings, without further proof or production of the originals. By the ninety-sixth section a certificate purporting to be under the hand of the Comptroller ... shall be prima-facie evidence of the entry having been made, and of the contents thereof, and of the matter or thing having been done or left undone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory seal and Comptroller's certification confer strong evidentiary status on Patent Office copies, registers, and certificates in legal proceedings across UK jurisdictions and the Isle of Man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposits and transmission of copies to repositories
rubrics_metrics.description: By the hundredth section ... copies of all specifications, drawings, and amendments left at the Patent Office ... printed for and sealed with the seal of the Patent Office, shall be transmitted to the Edinburgh Museum of Science and Art, and to the Enrolments Office of the Chancery Division in Ireland, and to the Rolls Office in the Isle of Man, within twenty-one days after the same shall respectively have been accepted or allowed at the Patent Office; and certified copies of or extracts from any such documents shall be given to any person requiring the same on payment of the prescribed fee; and any such copy or extract shall be admitted in evidence in all Courts in Scotland and Ireland and in the Isle of Man, without further proof or production of the originals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides administrative duties for distribution of official documents and confirms their admissibility in evidence outside England.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registers — public inspection and recorded matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The Register of Patents kept at the office ... is open to public inspection daily (with certain exceptions mentioned in Rule 78) between the hours of ten and four. Up to the end of 1883 the registers kept at the Patent Office were two. In the one called the Register of Patents were recorded, in chronological order and with the dates, all patents granted ... as well as the deposit or filing of specifications, disclaimers, memoranda of alterations, amendments, confirmations, and extensions, and the expiry, vacating, and cancelling of patents. The other register, called the Register of Proprietors, contains entries of the assignments of patents, or of any share or interest therein; and of licences, mentioning the districts to which they relate, with the names of persons having shares or interests in patents and licences, and the dates at which such shares or interests were acquired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registers serve as official public records for patent status, ownership, assignments, licences, and amendments; their contents are prima-facie evidence of matters directed to be inserted therein.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office publications and indexes — types and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides the Illustrated Official Journal relating to Patents and Reports of Patent Cases ... several other publications are issued by the Patent Office. A 'Circular of Information' ... Printed copies of all the specifications filed ... are purchasable ... Alphabetical indexes of all the specifications ... an index arranging the specifications according to the subject-matter, and supplemental indexes continue to be published annually. Chronological indexes of patents ... Another index, called the Reference Index of Patents, points out the office in which each enrolled or filed specification of a patent may be consulted ... The volumes containing abridgments of specifications arranged chronologically in classes are of immense utility ... but, unfortunately, these abridgments are not kept up to date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the official tools for searching prior art and patent history, their availability and limitations (e.g., abridgments not fully up to date). Copies of publications are presented to principal public offices and libraries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public library access
rubrics_metrics.description: A library has been established in connection with the Patent Office, and this is open free to the public. The whole of the publications of the office, and also the leading British and Foreign scientific journals and text-books in the various departments of science and art are in this library.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventors and agents may consult official publications and relevant scientific literature free at the Patent Office library to assist in preparing applications and searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Museum — requirement to furnish a model
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Museum at South Kensington is transferred ... to the Department of Science and Art, which is empowered ... to require any patentee to furnish them with a model of his invention on payment of the cost, the amount, in case of dispute, to be settled by the Board of Trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department may demand models for museum collections and the patentee must pay costs; Board of Trade resolves disputes over the amount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institute of Patent Agents — registration and qualifying examination
rubrics_metrics.description: By the first section of the Patents Act of 1888, it was enacted that after July 1st, 1889, a person shall not be entitled to describe himself as a Patent Agent ... unless he is registered as a Patent Agent in pursuance of that Act ... Every person who proves to the Board of Trade that he had been bona fide practising in the United Kingdom as a Patent Agent prior to the passing of the Act is entitled to be registered. With the exception of persons registered on this ground, no person is to be registered unless he has passed and produced to the Registrar a certificate under the seal of the Institute that he had passed such final examination as to his knowledge of Patent Law and Practice and of the duties of a Patent Agent as the Institute shall from time to time prescribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Institute manages registration and qualifying examinations; the Board of Trade issues rules. Grandfathering applies to bona fide practitioners prior to the Act upon proof; others must pass prescribed exams and produce the Institute's certificate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites and exemptions for the Patent Agent qualifying examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Before any person can present himself for the final qualifying examination of the Institute he must have passed one of the matriculation examinations of an English, Scottish, or Irish University, or the Oxford or Cambridge Middle Class Senior Local Examinations, or the Examinations of the Civil Service Commissioners, or such other examinations as the Institute shall, with the approval of the Board of Trade, prescribe. These preliminary examinations are not required in the case of solicitors in England and Ireland and law agents in Scotland, or in the case of persons who have for seven years been continuously engaged as pupils or assistants to registered Patent Agents. In these cases the final qualifying examination only is required to be passed by candidates for registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets educational prerequisites and professional exemptions (solicitors, law agents, long-serving pupils/assistants) for sitting the final qualifying exam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects and administration of the Institute's final qualifying examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The Institute must hold, at least once in the year, a final qualifying examination, and it is to have the entire management and conduct of such examination, including the appointment of the examiners. The subjects of examination are (a) Patent Law; (b) Patent practice and procedure; (c) the preparation and interpretation of patent documents; (d) physical science and its applications to the arts and manufactures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Candidates should apply to the Secretary of the Institute for further information; fees payable by a candidate, and those on registration and annually afterwards by Patent Agents are set forth in the Rules' Appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal from the register — misconduct and non-payment
rubrics_metrics.description: The names of persons convicted of crimes, or found guilty of disgraceful conduct, are to be removed from the register. Non-payment of fees is another cause for erasing the name of a Patent Agent from the register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Institute maintains professional discipline and financial compliance as grounds for erasure; a Registrar is appointed to keep the register under the direction of the Board of Trade.
